overview: Construction workers wave off the AI Plateau and stay mostly calm under Steady Disruption, sure that no robot can cope with a crooked wall or a wonky door frame any time soon, and most set out to learn the new kit. AGI by 2028 hits hardest: worry jumps to 3.5 out of 5, and most cut spending, save hard and lean on family, church, the union or the state. Given five or ten years they save and retrain at a steadier pace, and in every scenario adaptable workers with savings stay calmest while those who resist change and have little put by worry most.

S0.headline: Nearly every construction worker stays calm and carries on, treating AI as a handy tool for quotes and paperwork while the heavy, fiddly work stays in human hands.

whatTheyDo.text: Almost all of them keep working as now, finishing the current job and moving to the next, while chipping away at a mortgage, a van loan or an old boiler.
More than a third keep using AI for the dull bits, like cutting lists, quotes, method statements and kitchen layouts, and some ask for courses or extra pay for doing it.
About a quarter keep putting money aside, often a hundred or so a month for a house fund, a wedding or a plan to start their own firm.
About one in seven grow weekend work, such as decks, sheds, fences, garden offices or kitchen designs for neighbours.
Fewer than one in ten put money into the work itself or into savings plans, for example a van, a share in the firm, a laser scanner or an index fund.

S0.whatTheySay: Most say they never believed the fuss and that AI is a useful tool, not a miracle. Many joke that you still need someone to hang the doors, lift the joists in the rain or hang a ceiling at three in the morning.
S0.whatTheyThink: Privately most are relieved that their skills still count and their plans stay on track. Several say their real worries never had anything to do with AI: low-bid contracts, rent, a mortgage deal ending, or who'll carry on their craft after them.
S0.howTheyFeel: Calm and settled, a cup of tea kind of feeling. A few who built their edge on the new tools feel a little let down.

differences.text: Worry is the same for everyone, but adaptive workers keep learning AI tools far more (79%) than steady ones (30%), while no resistant ones do. Adaptive workers also grow side income (38%), which resistant ones don't.
Progressive workers are the only ones who push through the union (20%), and they use AI tools a bit more (48% against about 30%).
Workers with strong savings put less aside (11%) than those with thin or moderate savings (about 30%).

quotes.name: Wei Torres
quotes.text: The real work is still me and a nail gun.

quotes.name: Carla Diaz
quotes.text: Nobody's building a robot that can hang a ceiling at three in the morning in a shopping centre.

quotes.name: Ben Silva
quotes.text: If the boiler goes, we're on the credit card, and the boiler is fourteen years old.

S1.headline: Construction workers split evenly between calm and a little uneasy, and most set out to learn the new kit, often once they've seen it work on someone else's site.

whatTheyDo.text: Six in ten set out to learn the new tools, such as laser scanners, layout robots or planning apps, often signing up once a lead joiner or a couple of workmates have tried them.
Almost four in ten keep working as before, sticking to the parts that still need hands and leaving new gadgets to younger workmates or the boss's son.
About three in ten save a bit more just in case, for example raising savings to five months, holding off on a new van or pushing a house purchase back a year.
About three in ten hold back until they see machines on their own jobs, and only then decide whether to change anything.
More than a quarter turn to the union, going to every branch meeting and pushing for paid training, a list of who's at risk and no layoffs because a machine arrived.

S1.whatTheySay: Most take a practical line: some of it will stick and some won't, so learn the useful bits and don't panic. Many say offices will be hit long before building sites, and union voices want firms to pay for training rather than drop workers.
S1.whatTheyThink: Privately many expect repetitive work, like first fix, trusses and formwork, to move into factories, while repairs and old buildings stay human longest. Juniors and slower workers fear they'd be first to go, while gadget lovers see a chance to run the machines.
S1.howTheyFeel: Calm or mildly uneasy, a slow worry on the drive in. Those who already like the tech feel excited.

differences.text: Worry falls from 1.9 among resistant workers to 1.0 among adaptive ones. Resistant workers mostly keep going (84%) and wait and see (57%), while adaptive ones push for automation (62%), invest (49%) and grow side income (43%).
Progressive workers take collective action far more than anyone else (81%), while traditional ones are more likely to automate (32%) and invest (28%).
Worry falls from 1.8 for workers with thin savings to 1.4 for those with strong savings, and only those with thin savings cut spending much (21%).

quotes.name: Nikhil Khan
quotes.text: A machine can make a perfect door but someone has to plane it to fit a wonky frame.

quotes.name: Rosa Okafor
quotes.text: I'm the slowest one there, so if a program counts doors per hour, I'm the first name on the list.

quotes.name: Grace Novak
quotes.text: It's a good time to be curious and a bad time to be stubborn.

S2.headline: Most construction workers are anxious or alarmed, cutting back hard and leaning on family, church, the union or the state, because two years is far too fast to find new work.

whatTheyDo.text: Seven in ten cut back straight away, keeping only rent or the mortgage and food, and dropping the car, holidays, the gym or the kids' clubs. Some sell a van or a car to clear a loan.
About half put every spare amount into savings, for example cancelling a loft conversion or a summer holiday to stretch four months of bills towards six or a year.
Almost half look for help, such as moving into a parent's spare room, asking the church or grown children for support, or claiming every benefit through the council.
About a third push the union for redundancy terms, a wage guarantee during the changeover or retraining money, some giving up their Saturdays to campaign.
More than a quarter go after new work early, such as jobs setting up and running site robots, work for firms that sell or fit them, or any job still done by people.

S2.whatTheySay: Most say it's come far too fast and that firms and government must sit down and work out how people pay their bills. Many who don't usually want government help say this is like a flood. A few say don't wait to be saved, get moving.
S2.whatTheyThink: Privately many think they're finished in the trade, because the lifting and fixing they're good at is exactly what a robot would do first. Many fear both incomes in the house going at once, and worry about their apprentices, their kids and their village.
S2.howTheyFeel: Anxious or alarmed, often lying awake doing sums that don't add up. Some feel panicked, like standing on a roof after the ladder has gone.

differences.text: Worry rises from 2.9 among adaptive workers to 4.1 among resistant ones. Resistant workers cut spending (91%) and seek support (79%), while adaptive ones automate (54%), change jobs (41%) and invest (31%).
Worry rises from 3.1 for workers with strong savings to 4.0 for those with thin savings, who nearly all cut spending (94%), mostly seek support (67%) and are the most likely to change jobs (43%).
Progressive workers organise (95% take collective action) and turn to politics (67%), while traditional ones lean on family and church (69% seek support) and make family plans (36%).
Late-career workers worry a little less (3.4) and about one in five retire early (22%), while those in mid-career worry most (3.7).

quotes.name: Esther Evans
quotes.text: I'd probably say it as a joke first, "your mum's been made redundant by a toaster." Then I'd cry in the van after.

quotes.name: Tara Varga
quotes.text: I can learn a robot in a week. What I can't do is go three months without pay while I find the next thing.

quotes.name: Esther Ziegler
quotes.text: If a machine can do Henrik's work, and Peter's lorry drives itself, and the farmers don't need hands, what's a village for?

S3.headline: Construction workers still worry, but five years turns a cliff into a steep hill: most save hard and almost half start training for what comes next.

whatTheyDo.text: Three in four build up savings, for example cutting takeaways, holding off on a new kitchen or a house, or aiming for four to six months of cover by 2030.
Almost half train for something new, often a building inspection course, a site robotics certificate, heat pump or solar fitting, or a care certificate.
About three in ten plan around family, such as getting a partner to retrain first, steering a daughter towards nursing, or keeping the wedding but putting off the house.
About a quarter learn the robot software and new site systems, often once they're on proper sites, hoping to be the machine lead or the last foreman let go.
About a quarter build up a fallback, like weekend furniture or survey work, or a small business with a cutting machine that they could run full-time later.

S3.whatTheySay: Most say five years is fair warning if firms and government plan now, with paid training and proper apprenticeships in the new work. Some would wait a couple of years to see what really arrives.
S3.whatTheyThink: Privately many think the ending is the same, but they'd have time to move before the floor drops. Some see a chance to run robots or own a firm with them, while older workers hope to reach retirement, and some young ones find it almost crueller to get good just as it stops mattering.
S3.howTheyFeel: Mostly anxious or uneasy, a slow worry like watching water rise, but busy and with a plan to work on.

differences.text: Worry falls from 3.1 among resistant workers to 1.8 among adaptive ones. Resistant workers mostly save (98%) and keep going (49%) and hardly retrain (5%), while adaptive ones retrain (67%), automate (57%), invest (56%) and grow side income (51%).
Worry falls from 3.0 for thin savings to 2.1 for strong savings. Nearly everyone with a thin cushion saves (96%), while those with a strong one invest (37%) and plan around family (40%).
Progressive workers organise (72% take collective action) and retrain (63%), while traditional ones focus on family plans (42%), keep going (36%), invest (33%) and automate (33%).
Late-career workers worry least (2.4) and retrain less (33%) than early and mid-career workers (51%).

quotes.name: Sam Mensah
quotes.text: Two years was a cliff, five is a steep hill.

quotes.name: Iris Usman
quotes.text: With five years, maybe we're the family firm that owns a robot, not the family firm a robot put out of business.

quotes.name: Elena Jensen
quotes.text: Five years means I'm thirty-two and out of work instead of twenty-nine.

S4.headline: With ten years' warning most construction workers are calm or only a little uneasy, so they keep working, save steadily and plan around their families.

whatTheyDo.text: Almost six in ten carry on with their plans for now, getting their trade cards, leading their crews or working to retirement, and decide later.
Almost half save steadily, for example building six months of savings over five years or paying extra off the house.
About four in ten plan around family, such as helping a partner retrain first, buying a home on a short mortgage, or talking to the kids about subjects that will last.
Almost four in ten retrain at a calmer pace, often starting an inspection, supervisor or surveying course in year two to five once they see what's lasting.
About a quarter invest, such as buying robots in stages once they're proven and cheaper, setting up a co-op with rented machines, or paying more into a pension.

S4.whatTheySay: Most say ten years is plenty of warning, so there's no excuse for governments, firms or families not to plan, and training should start now. Some warn that ten years can turn into two very quickly.
S4.whatTheyThink: Privately many feel it's manageable: the mortgage nearly paid and the kids grown by then. Older workers expect to be retired and worry for their apprentices and grandchildren, while some keen workers expect to run robot crews, though they wonder what comes after that.
S4.howTheyFeel: Mostly uneasy or calm, a background worry they can live with, like a long drive in fog where they can still see some road.

differences.text: Worry falls from 2.3 among resistant workers to 1.2 among adaptive ones. Resistant workers nearly all keep going (93%) and many wait and see (41%), while adaptive ones grow side income (58%), invest (57%) and automate (41%).
Late-career workers worry least (1.5) and mostly keep going (86%). Mid-career workers worry most (1.9) and focus on family plans (65%), while early-career ones retrain most (56%).
Worry falls from 2.1 for thin savings to 1.5 for strong savings, and those with a thin cushion save far more (78% against 26%).
Progressive workers lean on collective action (51%) and politics (40%), while traditional ones put family plans first (58%) and automate more (30%).

quotes.name: Sam Haddad
quotes.text: It's still a big change, but it's one I could walk through instead of fall into.

quotes.name: Esther Torres
quotes.text: Time doesn't help me if I don't use it, and I don't.

quotes.name: Pedro Garcia
quotes.text: If a machine's going to take my job, I'd rather it was a machine I own a quarter of.
